conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the **EPDS** (the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because mood changes are incredibly common in the first months postpartum. Everything you share stays between you and your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll walk through ten gentle questions about the past seven days, and then we’ll talk about what the results might mean and any support you’d like. Ready to start?

In the past week, how often have you found yourself still able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy?

Honestly? Not very often. I still try—sometimes I’ll put on a podcast I used to love or take the baby out in the stroller—but it feels kind of flat, like I’m just going through the motions. Maybe once or twice I’ve caught myself half-smiling at something, but it’s nowhere near the way it used to feel.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I might let out a little laugh if my husband makes a joke, but it feels forced and fades right away. Most of the time nothing feels funny, and I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed without thinking about all the things I’m worried about.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much at all. When I think about plans—even little things like a coffee date or a walk—I mostly feel tired or wonder what’s the point. Once in a while I’ll look forward to maybe a TV show or a quiet moment, but it’s pretty rare and the excitement never lasts.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… more days than not, actually. If the baby fusses for a long time, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m not soothing him the way a “good mom” would. I replay little things in my head—like forgetting to bring a burp cloth or not noticing a diaper leak right away—and beat myself up for it, even when everyone says it’s normal.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. Even when everything looks fine—he’s breathing okay, sleeping okay—I still get this knot in my stomach that something bad could happen. I’ll check the monitor five times in ten minutes or Google symptoms that aren’t even there. It’s like my mind won’t let me relax without a reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… it’s happened a few times. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get a full breath, like I’m about to get bad news even though nothing’s happening. It passes after a few minutes, but in the moment it’s scary and I just want to hold the baby tight even though I know that’s probably not logical.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. Even simple stuff—folding a load of laundry or answering one text—can feel huge when the baby’s crying or I’m running on two hours of broken sleep. Sometimes I just sit there staring at nothing because I can’t figure out which thing to tackle first.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… pretty much every night this week. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with “what-ifs” about the baby. I’ll drift off and then jolt awake thinking I heard him cry, or just lie there feeling sad and heavy. It takes me at least an hour, sometimes more, to fall back asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty often—most days, really. It’s like this gray cloud that just hangs over everything. I’ll be feeding the baby or staring out the window and feel tears welling up without any clear reason. I wouldn’t say it’s every single moment, but it’s definitely more sad than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once was when I couldn’t get him to nap and I just felt like I was failing; the other was at night when I couldn’t sleep and all the worries piled up. The tears come pretty fast once they start, even though I try to hold them in so my husband doesn’t worry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

A couple of times, yeah. It’s more like a quick, scary picture that flashes—what if I just drove off the road or didn’t wake up. I don’t have any plan or real wish to do it; it just pops in and freaks me out. I’d never leave my baby, but the fact that the thought even shows up makes me feel awful.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Post-delivery mother (partner present), infant approx. 2–4 wks old  
Screening tool: EPDS-style interview (10 items) – self-report  
Date: _________  
Clinician: ________________  

Symptoms endorsed (≥ moderate–severe):  
- Marked anhedonia (items 1, 2)  
- Pervasive dysphoria, daily crying spells (items 8, 9)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to rumination (item 7)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame over routine infant care (item 3)  
- Chronic, ill-defined worry and catastrophic thinking; 2–3 panic-like episodes this week (items 4, 5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed / paralyzed by simple tasks; describes “treading water” (item 6)  

Pattern: Consistent with mixed depressive-anxiety presentation, postpartum onset.  

Safety: Passive self-harm ideation endorsed (“quick, scary picture” of driving off road, not waking up); denies intent or plan. States “I’d never leave my baby.” → Acute safety concern; requires formal risk assessment.  

Risk factors identified:  
- Insomnia & fatigue compounding mood liability  
- High self-expectations / perfectionism (“good mom” standard)  
- Limited perceived support (husband unaware of tearfulness)  
- History (not assessed today) of prior mood episodes, birth complications, or psychosocial stressors  

Screening impression:  
High likelihood of major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety, postpartum specifier. Meets threshold for immediate follow-up evaluation (diagnostic interview, safety plan, consider EPDS score ≥ 12–13). Recommend same-day referral to OB mental-health liaison or perinatal psychiatry for comprehensive assessment and safety planning.
